Build the lowest common denominator from the distinct factors rather than multiplying the denominators together
Multiply each numerator by whatever its own denominator was missing

Factorise the collected numerator and cancel it against the denominator
Recognise that a fully cancelled answer can be a plain number

Check a combined fraction by substituting a value of x into the original and the answer

sheet.howExamined: FM1 is a single 2-hour calculator paper of 100 marks with 12 to 15 questions. Combining algebraic fractions appeared in six of the eight series from 2018 to 2026 (2018, 2021, 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026), at Q7 to Q9, for 4 to 7 marks: Summer 2018 Q8(i) was 5 marks (MW1 for the factors, W1 for the cancelling, MW1 for the numerator, MW1 for the denominator, W1 for the answer) and was followed by a 'hence show that' equation and a completing-the-square part; Summer 2021 Q8(ii) was a 5-mark subtraction; Summer 2023 Q9 (4 marks) and Summer 2024 Q8(b) (5 marks) combined two fractions and then divided; Summer 2025 Q7 was 7 marks, a subtraction then a division marked M1 W1 M1 W1 MW1 W1 W1; Summer 2026 Q7(i) asked to show that a sum of two fractions set equal to 4 becomes a quadratic. Summer 2019 Q12(ii) placed the skill after an expansion.
traps: Subtracting a product without the minus reaching every term inside it (Summer 2025 Q7: the commonest mistake the report named)
Dropping the bracket round a subtracted numerator altogether (Summer 2025 Q7)
Using the product of the two denominators when one is a difference of two squares containing the other (Summer 2024 Q8(b), which produced cubics candidates could not work with)
Cancelling across the addition, before the two fractions have been combined (Summer 2024 Q8(b), Summer 2018 Q8)
Not factorising the quadratics at all, which leaves cubic numerators and denominators (Summer 2018 Q8)
Dividing the numerator by a constant before factorising it (Summer 2019 Q12(ii))
Stopping one line short of the final value, leaving the answer in factorised form (Summer 2025 Q7)
Failing to subtract every term of a quadratic from a cubic, when the question is an expansion followed by a subtraction (Summer 2022 Q9(a))

Leaving the combined fraction one step short of simplest form — factorise the numerator once the two fractions are over a common denominator, including when it turns out to be a difference of two squares, and cancel before the answer line (Summer 2023 Q9)

noteBlocks.lede: $\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{15}$ only adds once both are written in thirtieths. Algebraic fractions need the same thing, a common denominator, and factorising every denominator shows you what it is. After that the one real danger is the minus sign in front of a whole numerator.
can: Build the lowest common denominator from factorised denominators.
Subtract a whole numerator, changing every sign inside its bracket.
Finish by factorising the top and cancelling, even down to a number.

noteBlocks.md: Fractions only add when they share a denominator: $\frac{1}{6}+\frac{1}{15}$ becomes $\frac{5}{30}+\frac{2}{30}$. Algebraic fractions work the same way. The lowest common denominator is built from the brackets underneath, and each numerator is multiplied by the bracket its own fraction is missing, on the top and on the bottom at once.

steps.decision: The two denominators share no factor, so the lowest common denominator is their product. Leave it in brackets.
Each numerator is multiplied by the bracket its own fraction is missing: the 3 by $(x-4)$ and the 2 by $(x+1)$.
Expand and collect the top: $3x-12+2x+2 = 5x-10$.
Take out the common factor 5. No bracket on top matches one underneath, so this is the simplest form.

noteBlocks.prompt: Over $(x+2)(x-5)$, what is the numerator of $\dfrac{4}{x+2} + \dfrac{1}{x-5}$?
noteBlocks.explain: Each numerator takes the bracket its own fraction is missing, as step 2 of See it did: the 4 is missing $(x-5)$ and the 1 is missing $(x+2)$, so the top is $4(x-5)+(x+2)=5x-18$. $5x+3$ multiplies each by its own bracket; $5$ adds the tops without multiplying up.

twin.prompt: Over $(x+3)(x-4)$, what is the numerator of $\dfrac{2}{x+3} + \dfrac{3}{x-4}$?
twin.explain: The 2 is missing $(x-4)$ and the 3 is missing $(x+3)$, so the top is $2(x-4)+3(x+3)=5x+1$. $5x-6$ multiplies each by its own bracket; $5$ never multiplies up.

optionNotes.why: Each top was multiplied by its own bracket, which is already there; it needs the missing one.
The tops were added without being multiplied up to the common denominator.
It feels natural to pair each top with the bracket under it, but that bracket is already there: each top needs the one it is missing.
Adding the tops is tempting because the fractions now share a bottom, but the tops were never multiplied up to match it.

noteBlocks.md: Multiplying the top and the bottom of $\frac{3}{x+1}$ by $(x-4)$ multiplies the fraction by $\frac{x-4}{x-4}$, which is 1 for every $x$ except 4. So its value never changes; only the way it is written does.
That gives you a free check on any answer. Put a number in for $x$, one that makes no denominator zero, into the question and into your single fraction: the two values must agree.

steps.decision: Put $x = 1$ into the question.
Put $x = 1$ into the answer. The two agree, so the working holds.
A slip shows at once: multiplying each top by its own bracket gives $\frac{5x-5}{(x+1)(x-4)}$, which is 0 at $x = 1$, not $\frac{5}{6}$.

noteBlocks.prompt: At $x = 4$, $\dfrac{2}{x-3} + \dfrac{1}{x+2}$ equals $\dfrac{13}{6}$. Which could be its single fraction?
noteBlocks.explain: Multiplying up never changes a value, so the right single fraction also gives $\frac{13}{6}$ at $x = 4$, as the check in See it did. $\frac{3x+1}{(x-3)(x+2)}$ gives $\frac{13}{6}$. $\frac{3x-4}{(x-3)(x+2)}$ gives $\frac{8}{6}$ (each top took its own bracket) and $\frac{3}{(x-3)(x+2)}$ gives $\frac{3}{6}$ (nothing multiplied up).

twin.prompt: At $x = 4$, $\dfrac{3}{x+1} + \dfrac{1}{x-3}$ equals $\dfrac{8}{5}$. Which could be its single fraction?
twin.explain: The right fraction keeps the value, $\frac{8}{5}$ at $x = 4$: $\frac{4x-8}{(x+1)(x-3)}$ does. $\frac{4x}{(x+1)(x-3)}$ gives $\frac{16}{5}$ and $\frac{4}{(x+1)(x-3)}$ gives $\frac{4}{5}$.

optionNotes.why: Each top took its own bracket, so the value changes: at x = 4 it gives 16/5, not 8/5.
Nothing was multiplied up, so the value falls to 4/5.
Each top took its own bracket, which changes both fractions' values, so the check at x = 4 no longer agrees.
Nothing was multiplied up, so the value falls: at x = 4 it gives 3/6, not 13/6.

noteBlocks.md: When the numerators are brackets too, nothing new happens: each numerator is still multiplied by the bracket its fraction is missing. Now each part of the top is a product of two brackets, so expand them one at a time, each on its own line, and only then collect. The 2026 paper set this shape and then put the result equal to a number, so the top has to be exactly right.

steps.decision: Nothing is shared underneath, so the lowest common denominator is the product.
Each numerator takes the bracket its fraction is missing: $(2x+1)$ takes $(x-1)$ and $(x-2)$ takes $(x+3)$.
Expand the first product on its own line.
Then the second, on its own line.
Add the two: $2x^{2}+x^{2}=3x^{2}$, the $x$ terms cancel, and $-1-6=-7$. The top does not factorise, so this is the answer.

noteBlocks.prompt: Over $(x+4)(x-2)$, what is the numerator of $\dfrac{x+1}{x+4} + \dfrac{x+3}{x-2}$?
noteBlocks.explain: Each top takes the bracket its fraction is missing, as step 2 of See it did, so the numerator is $(x+1)(x-2)+(x+3)(x+4)$. Expanding one product at a time gives $x^{2}-x-2$ and $x^{2}+7x+12$, so $2x^{2}+6x+10$. $2x^{2}+6x-2$ used each fraction's own bracket; $2x+4$ added the tops as they stood.

twin.prompt: Over $(x+1)(x-3)$, what is the numerator of $\dfrac{x+2}{x+1} + \dfrac{x-4}{x-3}$?
twin.explain: The numerator is $(x+2)(x-3)+(x-4)(x+1)$, each top times the bracket it was missing. That is $x^{2}-x-6$ plus $x^{2}-3x-4$, so $2x^{2}-4x-10$. $2x^{2}-4x+14$ used the wrong brackets; $2x-2$ never multiplied up.

optionNotes.why: Each top was multiplied by its own bracket instead of the one it was missing.
The tops were added as they stood, never multiplied up.
Multiplying each top by its own bracket looks tidy, but it changes both fractions: each top takes the bracket it is missing.
Adding the tops as they stand skips the multiplying up that the common denominator demands.

noteBlocks.md: When a fraction is subtracted, the whole of its multiplied-up numerator is taken away. So write the minus sign and then that numerator inside a bracket. Expand inside the bracket on its own line, and only then remove the bracket, changing the sign of every term inside it.

noteBlocks.title: Summer 2025, FM1 Q7
noteBlocks.md: Most candidates found the common denominator on this seven-mark question, yet very few scored full marks. The mistake the report put first was a minus sign that did not reach every term of a subtracted product.

steps.decision: Nothing is shared underneath, so the lowest common denominator is the product.
The subtracted numerator keeps its bracket, with the minus in front of the whole of it.
Expand inside the bracket first, and keep the bracket.
Now remove the bracket: all three signs change, so $-2$ becomes $+2$.
Take out the common factor 2; no bracket matches one underneath.

noteBlocks.title: Adding Algebraic Fractions
noteBlocks.why: Seven minutes of further examples over a common denominator, subtraction included, if you want another voice before your turn.

noteBlocks.explain: Expand inside the bracket first, as step 3 of See it did: $(x+1)(x-3)=x^{2}-2x-3$. Taking all of it away changes every sign: $x^{2}+6x-x^{2}+2x+3=8x+3$. $4x-3$ changed the first sign only; $2x^{2}+4x-3$ added instead of taking away.

twin.explain: $(x+2)(x-5)=x^{2}-3x-10$, and all of it is taken away, so every sign changes: $x^{2}+2x-x^{2}+3x+10=5x+10$. $-x-10$ changed the first sign only; $2x^{2}-x-10$ added the bracket.

optionNotes.why: The minus reached only the first term of the bracket.
The bracket was added instead of taken away.
The minus reached the first term and stopped; it belongs to every term inside the bracket.
With the bracket dropped the minus is lost, so the product was added instead of taken away.

noteBlocks.caption: Factorised, $x^{2}-49$ already holds $(x-7)$, so the lowest common denominator is $(x+7)(x-7)$ and nothing more.

noteBlocks.md: Factorise every denominator before you choose. If $x^{2}-49$ stands beside $x-7$, then $x^{2}-49=(x+7)(x-7)$ already contains $(x-7)$, so the lowest common denominator is $(x+7)(x-7)$: each distinct bracket once.

Multiplying the two printed denominators together also gives a common denominator, but a cubic one, and the extra bracket has to be cancelled again at the end. In Summer 2024 candidates who took that route were left with cubics they could not finish.

steps.decision: Factorise the quadratic denominator first: a difference of two squares.
$(x-7)$ is already inside the other denominator, so the LCD is $(x+7)(x-7)$; only the 3 needs multiplying up.
Expand and collect: $3x+21+x+1$.
Take out the common factor 2. Neither bracket underneath matches, so nothing cancels.

noteBlocks.prompt: What is the lowest common denominator of $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}-100}$ and $\dfrac{1}{x+10}$?
noteBlocks.explain: Factorise first, as step 1 of See it did: $x^{2}-100=(x+10)(x-10)$, and $(x+10)$ is already one of those brackets, so each distinct bracket once gives $(x+10)(x-10)$. $(x+10)^{2}(x-10)$ multiplies the printed denominators: common, but not lowest. $x^{2}+x-90$ adds them, which is never how fractions combine.

twin.prompt: What is the lowest common denominator of $\dfrac{1}{x^{2}-144}$ and $\dfrac{1}{x-12}$?
twin.explain: $x^{2}-144=(x+12)(x-12)$ already holds $(x-12)$, so the lowest common denominator is $(x+12)(x-12)$. $(x+12)(x-12)^{2}$ is the product of the printed denominators; $x^{2}+x-156$ adds them.

optionNotes.why: That is the product of the printed bottoms: common, but it holds a bracket twice.
Denominators never combine by adding.
Multiplying the two printed bottoms always gives a common denominator, but it holds a bracket twice, so it is not the lowest.
Adding the bottoms feels like combining them, but denominators combine through their factors, never by adding.

noteBlocks.caption: Strike the bracket the top and bottom share inside the first fraction, before any adding.

noteBlocks.md: Sometimes one fraction simplifies on its own before any adding. Factorise its top and its bottom, and divide out a bracket they share. Doing it first shrinks the common denominator and every numerator after it. The Summer 2018 scheme gave a mark for that cancel, and candidates who skipped it ended up with cubics on both lines.

noteBlocks.title: Why two denominators never cancel
noteBlocks.md: Cancelling divides the top and the bottom of one fraction by the same thing, which leaves its value alone. Two denominators belong to two different fractions, so striking a bracket from both divides neither fraction by anything: it changes both values.

noteBlocks.stem: Express $\dfrac{x^{2}+4x-5}{x(x+5)} + \dfrac{3x}{x+4}$ as one fraction in its simplest form.

steps.decision: Factorise the quadratic top: two numbers with product $-5$ and sum $4$.
$(x+5)$ is a factor of the top and the bottom of this one fraction, so it divides out before any adding.
Now add. The LCD is $x(x+4)$: the first top takes $(x+4)$ and the second takes $x$.
Expand and collect: $x^{2}+3x-4+3x^{2}$. The top does not factorise, so nothing more cancels.

noteBlocks.prompt: Before any adding, what does $\dfrac{x^{2}+x-12}{x(x+4)}$ become?
noteBlocks.explain: Factorise the top, as steps 1 and 2 of See it did: $x^{2}+x-12=(x+4)(x-3)$, and $(x+4)$ is also underneath, so it divides out, leaving $\frac{x-3}{x}$. $\frac{x-12}{4x}$ strikes the $x^{2}$ terms, which are terms of a sum; saying it does not simplify misses the shared bracket.

twin.prompt: Before any adding, what does $\dfrac{x^{2}+2x-8}{x(x+4)}$ become?
twin.explain: $x^{2}+2x-8=(x+4)(x-2)$, and $(x+4)$ is underneath too, so it divides out: $\frac{x-2}{x}$. $\frac{2x-8}{4x}$ strikes terms; the shared bracket means it does simplify.

optionNotes.why: That strikes terms of a sum, not a shared factor.
Factorised, the top $(x+4)(x-2)$ shares $(x+4)$ with the bottom.
Striking the $x^{2}$ terms looks like cancelling, but they are terms of a sum; only a factor of the whole top and bottom can go.
It looks stuck until the top is factorised: $(x+4)(x-3)$ shares $(x+4)$ with the bottom.

noteBlocks.md: A plain number can sit underneath too. For $\frac{x}{5}$ and $\frac{5}{x}$ the lowest common denominator is $5x$: the 5 is missing an $x$, and the $x$ is missing a 5. The top that comes out is often a difference of two squares, and it must be factorised, because the next line of the question usually cancels one of its brackets. Summer 2023 candidates who did not spot it could not cancel.

noteBlocks.stem: Write $\dfrac{x}{5} - \dfrac{5}{x}$ as one fraction, fully factorised.

steps.decision: The 5 and the $x$ share nothing, so the lowest common denominator is their product.
The first top is missing an $x$ and the second a 5.
Multiply out the top.
$x^{2}-25$ is a difference of two squares, so it factorises; the brackets are ready to cancel in a next line.

noteBlocks.explain: The lowest common denominator is $8x$, as in step 1 of See it, and each top takes what its fraction is missing: $x \times x - 8 \times 8 = x^{2}-64 = (x+8)(x-8)$. $\frac{x-8}{8x}$ never multiplied the tops up; $\frac{x^{2}-64}{x+8}$ added the denominators.

twin.explain: Over $10x$ the top is $x^{2}-100=(x+10)(x-10)$. $\frac{x-10}{10x}$ never multiplied up; $\frac{x^{2}-100}{x+10}$ added the denominators.

optionNotes.why: The tops were never multiplied up to the common denominator 10x.
Adding the bottoms is never how fractions combine.
Subtracting the tops as they stand forgets that each must first take what its bottom is missing.
Adding the bottoms is never how fractions combine; the common denominator here is their product, 8x.

noteBlocks.md: The last mark nearly always sits here. When the top is collected, factorise it (a common factor first, then the quadratic) and compare each bracket with the ones underneath. A bracket on both lines divides out.
Never divide the top by a number on its own first: that changes the fraction. Summer 2019 candidates who divided a collected numerator by 3 before factorising lost the final mark.

steps.decision: Factorise the quadratic denominator first.
$(x-5)$ is shared, so the LCD is $(x-5)(x+2)$ and only the $x$ is multiplied up.
Expand and collect the top.
Factorise the top: two numbers with product $-35$ and sum $2$.
$(x-5)$ is on both lines, so it divides out.

noteBlocks.prompt: A fraction's top has come out as $3x^{2}-3x-18$ and its bottom is $(x+2)(x+4)$. What do you do next?
options: Leave it: a quadratic numerator cannot cancel with a product of brackets
noteBlocks.explain: Factorise the top before anything else, as steps 4 and 5 of See it did: the common factor 3 first, then the quadratic, so $3x^{2}-3x-18=3(x+2)(x-3)$, and $(x+2)$ is also underneath, so it divides out. Dividing the top alone by 3 changes the fraction; a quadratic top can cancel as soon as it is factorised.

twin.prompt: A fraction's top has come out as $2x^{2}+2x-24$ and its bottom is $(x+4)(x+1)$. What do you do next?
options: Leave it: a quadratic numerator cannot cancel with a product of brackets
twin.explain: Common factor first, then the quadratic: $2x^{2}+2x-24=2(x+4)(x-3)$, and $(x+4)$ is underneath too, so it divides out. Dividing the top alone by 2 changes the fraction.

optionNotes.why: Dividing the top alone by 2 changes the fraction's value.

optionNotes.option: Leave it: a quadratic numerator cannot cancel with a product of brackets
optionNotes.why: Factorised, the top shares a bracket with the bottom.
Dividing the top alone by 3 feels like simplifying, but it changes the fraction's value; factorise and let the 3 stay.

optionNotes.option: Leave it: a quadratic numerator cannot cancel with a product of brackets
optionNotes.why: A quadratic top can hide a bracket the bottom shares; factorising it is exactly how you find out.

noteBlocks.caption: Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by it turned upside down: its top and bottom swap.

noteBlocks.md: The seven-mark version combines two fractions inside a bracket and then divides by a third. Finish the bracket first, with its top collected and factorised. Then turn the dividing fraction upside down and multiply, factorising its quadratic too.

Often every bracket pairs off and the answer is a plain number. That is not a mistake: in Summer 2025 the last mark went to the candidates who wrote that number down instead of stopping one line short.

steps.decision: The bracket first: over its LCD, the subtracted top keeps its bracket.
Expand inside the bracket, then change every sign as it comes off.
Dividing by a fraction is multiplying by it turned upside down.
Factorise the new quadratic: the common factor 2 first.
Every bracket pairs off and 2 is left: that plain number is the answer.

noteBlocks.prompt: A bracket has come to $\dfrac{3x+1}{(x-1)(x+3)}$. It is divided by $\dfrac{3x+1}{4x^{2}+8x-12}$. What is the result?
noteBlocks.explain: Turn the dividing fraction upside down and multiply, as step 3 of See it did, then factorise: $4x^{2}+8x-12=4(x-1)(x+3)$, so every bracket pairs off and 4 is left. $\frac{1}{4}$ turned the wrong fraction over; the long fraction multiplied without turning over.

twin.prompt: A bracket has come to $\dfrac{2x+5}{(x+2)(x-2)}$. It is divided by $\dfrac{2x+5}{3x^{2}-12}$. What is the result?
twin.explain: Turn the divisor over and multiply: $3x^{2}-12=3(x+2)(x-2)$, so everything pairs off and 3 is left. $\frac{1}{3}$ turned the wrong fraction over; the long fraction never turned over.

optionNotes.why: The wrong fraction was turned over, giving the reciprocal.
The divisor was multiplied as it stood, never turned over.
That turned the bracket's fraction over instead of the one you divide by, so you reached the reciprocal of the answer.
That multiplies by the divisor as it stands; a division turns the second fraction upside down first.

noteBlocks.md: **Simplest form means fully.** "One fraction in its simplest form" (2018) asks what "simplify fully" asks (2021, 2023 to 2025): the top collected and factorised, anything shared cancelled.
**The answer can be a number.** When every bracket pairs off, the answer is a plain number (2025's seven-mark question ended on one): write it on the answer line.

**It becomes an equation.** A part may ask you to show that the fraction, set equal to a number, gives a quadratic (2018, 2026): put your single fraction equal to the number, then multiply both sides by its whole denominator.
**The top comes from an earlier part.** After an expansion (2019), bracket every term you take away before you collect and factorise the new numerator.

noteBlocks.stem: Show that $\dfrac{3x^{2}-7}{(x+3)(x-1)} = 2$ can be written as $x^{2}-4x-1=0$.

steps.decision: Multiply both sides by the whole denominator: the cross-multiplying the scheme credits.
Expand the right-hand side.
Collect everything on one side: the printed equation, so the show is complete.

noteBlocks.prompt: A part says: show that $\dfrac{4x+5}{(x+2)(x-1)} = 3$ can be written as $3x^{2}-x-11=0$. What is your first line?
noteBlocks.explain: Clear the fraction by multiplying both sides by the whole denominator, as step 1 of See it did: $4x+5=3(x+2)(x-1)$, which expands and collects to $3x^{2}-x-11=0$. $4x+5=3$ drops the denominator; multiplying only the left side by it changes the equation.

twin.prompt: A part says: show that $\dfrac{2x+7}{(x+1)(x-2)} = 2$ can be written as $2x^{2}-4x-11=0$. What is your first line?
twin.explain: Multiply both sides by the whole denominator: $2x+7=2(x+1)(x-2)$, which collects to $2x^{2}-4x-11=0$. $2x+7=2$ drops the denominator; the third line multiplies one side only.

optionNotes.why: The denominator was dropped instead of multiplying both sides by it.
Only one side was multiplied by the denominator.
Dropping the denominator makes the line look simpler, but both sides must be multiplied by it, not the fraction just deleted.
Multiplying only the left side by the denominator changes the equation; the right-hand number is multiplied too.

noteBlocks.md: The hardest shape, set in 2018, chains four moves: cancel inside one fraction, add the two, put the result equal to a number, then solve the quadratic that comes out by completing the square. Each part feeds the next, so check each line with a number before you move on.

noteBlocks.title: Beyond this specification
noteBlocks.md: Splitting one fraction back into two (partial fractions) is A-level work: no FM1 question asks for it.

steps.decision: Cancel inside the first fraction: $(x+5)$ is on its top and its bottom.
Add over the LCD $x(x+4)$, then expand and collect the top.
Put it equal to 2 and multiply both sides by the whole denominator.
Expand and collect: $3x^{2}-2x^{2}=x^{2}$ and $2x-8x=-6x$.
Complete the square: half of $-6$ is $-3$, and $-9-8=-17$.
Square root both sides, keeping both signs.

noteBlocks.prompt: $\dfrac{x-1}{x} + \dfrac{2x}{x+2} = 2$. Which quadratic equation does it become?
noteBlocks.explain: Add over $x(x+2)$ to get $\frac{3x^{2}+x-2}{x(x+2)}$, then multiply both sides by that whole denominator, as steps 2 to 4 of See it did: $3x^{2}+x-2=2x(x+2)$ collects to $x^{2}-3x-2=0$. $3x^{2}+x-4=0$ never multiplied the 2; $3x^{2}-x-2=0$ multiplied it by $x$ alone.

twin.prompt: $\dfrac{x-4}{x} + \dfrac{2x}{x+1} = 2$. Which quadratic equation does it become?
twin.explain: Over $x(x+1)$ the top is $3x^{2}-3x-4$; multiplying both sides by $x(x+1)$ gives $3x^{2}-3x-4=2x(x+1)$, so $x^{2}-5x-4=0$. The other two forgot to multiply the 2 by the whole denominator.

optionNotes.why: The 2 on the right was not multiplied by the denominator.
The 2 was multiplied by x alone, not the whole denominator.
The fraction was cleared but the 2 on the right was not multiplied by the denominator as well.
The 2 was multiplied by x alone; the whole denominator, x(x + 2), multiplies both sides.

noteBlocks.md: Every example above uses one rule. Multiplying the first fraction by $\frac{d}{d}$ and the second by $\frac{b}{b}$ changes neither, because each is 1, and it puts both over $bd$. Then the tops combine. When $b$ and $d$ share a factor, $bd$ is still a common denominator, just not the lowest.

steps.decision: Multiply the top and the bottom by $d$: that is multiplying by 1.
Multiply the top and the bottom by $b$.
Same denominator, so subtract the tops.
With $a=3$, $b=x+1$, $c=2$ and $d=x-4$, the rule writes the line you start with.

noteBlocks.prompt: By the same rule, what is $\dfrac{p}{q} + \dfrac{r}{s}$?
noteBlocks.explain: Give each fraction the other's denominator by multiplying by 1, as steps 1 and 2 of See it did: $\frac{p}{q}=\frac{ps}{qs}$ and $\frac{r}{s}=\frac{qr}{qs}$, so the sum is $\frac{ps+qr}{qs}$. Adding tops and bottoms separately changes the values; $\frac{pr}{qs}$ is the product, not the sum.

twin.prompt: By the same rule, what is $\dfrac{m}{n} - \dfrac{k}{t}$?

items.stem: You are subtracting one algebraic fraction from another. What must go round the second numerator?

options.text: A bracket, with the minus sign in front of it
options.feedback: Then when the bracket comes off, every sign inside it changes. It is one extra pair of symbols and it is the difference between full marks and five out of seven.

options.text: Nothing — write the terms straight down after the minus sign
options.feedback: Then the minus reaches only the first term. Summer 2025 examiners named this as the commonest error on the whole question.

options.text: A bracket round the first term only
options.feedback: The whole of the second numerator is being taken away, so the whole of it goes inside the bracket.

items.skill: Apply a minus sign across a whole product

options.feedback: $(x-3)(x+3)$ expands to $x^{2}-9$, and taking all of it away changes all three signs.
Only the first term of the bracket had its sign changed, and the minus reaches every term. A minus that missed part of a subtracted bracket was the mistake the Summer 2025 report put first.
The bracket was dropped and the two numerators were added instead of subtracted. Write the minus and the bracket together, before you expand anything.

items.stem: Written as one fraction, what is $\dfrac{2}{x} + \dfrac{3}{x+1}$?
items.skill: Multiply each numerator up to the common denominator

options.feedback: Over $x(x+1)$ the numerators become $2(x+1) + 3x$, which collects to $5x+2$.
The tops were added and the bottoms were added. Fractions are never combined that way: they need a common denominator first.
The common denominator is right and the numerators were never multiplied up to match it. Each numerator is multiplied by whatever its own denominator was missing.

items.stem: In $\dfrac{x}{x^{2}-9} + \dfrac{2}{x-3}$, may you cancel the $(x-3)$ in the first denominator against the $(x-3)$ in the second?
items.skill: Refuse to cancel across an addition

options.text: No — cancelling needs a factor of a numerator and a factor of a denominator
options.feedback: Both of those are denominators, and they belong to different fractions that have not been combined yet. Cancelling only happens inside one fraction.

options.text: Yes, because the same bracket appears twice
options.feedback: Appearing twice is not enough. Summer 2024 examiners described incorrect cancelling before the addition as one of the disappointing features of that question.

options.text: Yes, but only after the numerators have been added
options.feedback: Once the fractions are combined there is one numerator and one denominator, and then you cancel factors of those. The two denominators themselves never cancel each other.

items.stem: You have combined two fractions and collected the numerator. What is the last thing to do?
items.skill: Factorise the numerator and look for a cancel

options.text: Factorise the numerator and see whether anything cancels with the denominator
options.feedback: It is the last mark on nearly every one of these questions, and it is the one Summer 2025 reported as most often missed.

options.text: Nothing — a collected numerator over the common denominator is the answer
options.feedback: Sometimes it is, and you only know by trying to factorise. When the numerator does factorise, one of its brackets is usually the one underneath.

options.text: Multiply the denominator out so the answer is a single quadratic over a single quadratic
options.feedback: Multiplying the denominator out hides the very factor you are looking for. Leave it in brackets.

items.stem: What is the numerator of $\dfrac{x}{x-3} - \dfrac{18}{x^{2}-9}$ once both fractions are over $(x-3)(x+3)$?

options.feedback: $x(x+3) - 18$, which expands and collects to $x^{2}+3x-18$, and that factorises as $(x+6)(x-3)$.
The numerators were subtracted as they stood. The first fraction's denominator is missing $(x+3)$, so its numerator has to be multiplied by it.
The multiplying up is right and the second numerator was added rather than taken away. Write the minus sign and the bracket together before you expand anything.

options.feedback: Over $(x-6)(x+6)$ the top is $5(x+6)-60=5x-30=5(x-6)$, and $(x-6)$ cancels.
Everything up to here is right. The top factorises as $5(x-6)$ and one bracket cancels: that is the last mark.
The two printed denominators were multiplied instead of $x^{2}-36$ being factorised first. The value is right; the fraction is nowhere near its simplest form.

options.feedback: $x^{2}-2x-15=(x-5)(x+3)$, and $(x-5)$ is also underneath, so it divides out.

That strikes the $x^{2}$ terms, which are terms of a sum: $\frac{x^{2}-2x-15}{x^{2}-5x}$ with them struck leaves $\frac{-2x-15}{-5x}$. Only a factor of the whole top and the whole bottom can go, so factorise first.

findings.asked: Combine algebraic fractions with quadratic denominators, then use the result.
findings.wentWrong: Many did not factorise the quadratics first and ended up with cubic numerators and denominators; incorrect cancelling appeared inside the addition; a follow-through mark was available for cross-multiplying.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Factorised every quadratic, identified the lowest common denominator, combined, and cancelled only at the end.

findings.asked: Expand a product, then substitute it into a numerator and simplify a fraction.
findings.wentWrong: Gathering the terms in the numerator went wrong, and those with the right numerator often divided by 3 before factorising, producing a wrong final form.
findings.rule: Factorise the numerator before dividing anything out.

findings.asked: Simplify a fraction, then add two algebraic fractions.
findings.wentWrong: In the addition, x squared - 9 was seen as a difference of two squares but (x + 3)(x - 3) was not used as the common denominator, so cubics appeared; some cancelled terms before adding; the simplification missed a factor of 2.
findings.rule: After a difference of two squares the LCD is the pair of brackets, not the product of the denominators.

findings.asked: Combine and simplify two algebraic fractions to a constant.
findings.wentWrong: Most reached 5 of 7 marks; the killer error was subtracting a bracketed product and changing only its first term's sign; brackets dropped; premature cancelling; stopping before the final value.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the subtracted product in brackets, expanded it in full, applied the minus to every term, collected, factorised and cancelled to the final value.
findings.rule: Minus a bracket: every term changes sign.

insight.ruleToRemember: Factorise every numerator and denominator; the LCD is the product of the distinct factors; keep subtracted numerators in brackets and distribute the sign; cancel only whole factors, and simplify to the end.
insight.aStarSignal: An addition where the LCD comes from a difference of two squares and the numerator must be subtracted with a sign change on every term, finishing as a single simplified expression.
